strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and previously underexplored question: whether CLIP's bag-of-words behavior stems from missing attribute-object binding information or from poor cross-modal alignment, disentangling these two hypotheses via careful unimodal analysis.

Multiple converging lines of evidence (linear probing, robustness to increasing object count, conjunctive search experiments, and a BoW-constrained control model) all support the central claim that binding information is linearly present within each modality but not aligned across modalities.

Proposes a practical, lightweight solution (LABCLIP) that requires no retraining of CLIP's encoders, is backward compatible with existing embedding databases, and is much more efficient to train than full fine-tuning (NegCLIP), while achieving competitive gains on both synthetic and real-world compositional benchmarks.
Introduces a new synthetic dataset (PUG:SPARE) that removes a positional shortcut present in PUG:SPAR, improving the rigor of unimodal binding evaluation.

Thorough experimentation across multiple CLIP backbones (ViT-B/32, B/16, L/14), several datasets (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE, ARO, SugarCrepe, COCO, CC3M), and extensive appendix analyses (modality gap, representational similarity, spatial reasoning transfer, downstream task trade-offs).
Clear presentation with intuitive figures (Fig. 1, 3, 5, 6) that effectively communicate the core hypothesis and findings.
weaknesses: The core positive findings rely heavily on small-scale, simplified synthetic datasets (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE) with limited numbers of objects/attributes; it is unclear how well the unimodal binding claims generalize to complex, naturalistic scenes with richer compositional structure.

LABCLIP's improvements on real-world benchmarks (Table 4) are only roughly comparable to NegCLIP and sometimes lower, while it also reduces zero-shot performance on single-object classification tasks (CIFAR, ImageNet, Table 11), indicating a nontrivial trade-off that is not fully resolved or mitigated.

The BoW-model sanity check (training CLIP-like encoders with soft-label attribute prediction) is a somewhat artificial construction and may not perfectly capture what 'true BoW representations' would look like, so its power as a control is limited.

Image embedding binding degrades notably with increasing object count (Fig. 4), which somewhat weakens the strength of the 'uni-modal binding is robust' claim, particularly for the visual modality in cluttered scenes.

The proposed alignment method (a global linear transformation) is conceptually simple and its novelty relative to prior negative-pair fine-tuning approaches (e.g., NegCLIP) is incremental; the primary contribution is more diagnostic/analytical than methodological.
Real-world evaluation is restricted mainly to ARO, SugarCrepe, and COCO/CC3M training; broader benchmarks (e.g., Winoground, VL-Checklist, CREPE) are not evaluated, limiting generality claims.

Linear probing accuracy demonstrating 'information is present' does not fully establish that this information is causally used or easily exploitable in downstream inference; alternative confounds (e.g., subtle positional or compositional cues not fully eliminated) could partially explain probe success.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and well-motivated question: whether CLIP's BoWness stems from missing binding information in the encoders or from cross-modal misalignment. This is a clean, well-posed research question that previous work had not clearly disentangled.

The experimental methodology is thorough and multi-pronged: linear probing on individual modalities, robustness tests with increasing object counts, and a conjunctive search experiment adapted from Campbell et al. (2024). These complementary approaches converge on the same conclusion, strengthening the evidentiary basis for the paper's claims.
The introduction of PUG:SPARE to remove positional shortcut bias present in PUG:SPAR is a thoughtful methodological contribution that improves the validity of the uni-modal binding experiments.

The proposed LABCLIP method is simple, practical, and well-motivated by the paper's diagnostic findings. It is lightweight (only a linear transformation), computationally efficient (100x faster than NegCLIP), and backward-compatible with existing CLIP vector databases, which has clear practical value.

Extensive appendix experiments (different backbones, aligning image vs text space, spatial reasoning evaluation, downstream task tradeoffs, modality gap analysis, probe coefficient similarity analysis) substantially bolster the robustness and credibility of the core claims.
The sanity check with a trained BoW-constrained CLIP encoder (achieving much lower probing accuracy) is a nice control that strengthens the interpretation of the linear probing results.

Results are validated on both controlled synthetic datasets (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE) and real-world benchmarks (ARO, SugarCrepe, COCO), showing the findings generalize beyond synthetic controlled settings.
The paper is clearly written with intuitive figures (e.g., Fig. 1, Fig. 3) that effectively communicate the core hypothesis and findings.
weaknesses: The synthetic datasets (CLEVR, PUG:SPAR/SPARE) are limited to two-object scenes for most core experiments (§4.1, §5), and the multi-object robustness test (§4.2) is only conducted on CLEVR with simple shapes/colors, leaving open questions about how binding degrades in more complex, cluttered real-world images with many objects and diverse attributes.

LABCLIP's real-world gains (Table 4) are comparable to but not exceeding NegCLIP, and the paper reports a tradeoff where LABCLIP reduces zero-shot single-object classification accuracy (Table 11) — this practical cost to downstream performance deserves more thorough investigation or mitigation strategies rather than being noted briefly.

The linear probing approach, while informative, has known limitations as a method for establishing 'information content' — linear separability does not necessarily equate to the information being usable in the same way the model would need for cross-modal matching; the paper could more rigorously discuss why linear probing is a sufficient proxy for the claim that CLIP 'has' binding information.

The image modality's binding signal degrades notably with more objects (from ~0.9 to ~0.6 accuracy in Fig. 4), which somewhat weakens the strength of the uni-modal binding claim for images in cluttered scenes, though the paper does acknowledge this.

The paper's explanation for why cross-modal alignment fails to preserve binding (i.e., why CLIP's contrastive objective doesn't incentivize alignment of binding-specific structure) remains largely hypothesized rather than directly tested via, e.g., controlled ablations on the training objective or gradient analysis.

Some real-world results (e.g., LABCLIP trained on CC3M performing worse on compositional benchmarks) are attributed to dataset similarity effects citing Oh et al. (2024), but this alternative explanation is not tested directly within the paper's own experimental framework.
